A herpetologist is a scientist who studies reptiles and amphibians — two distinct groups of cold-blooded animals.

Reptiles include animals like snakes, lizards, crocodiles, turtles, and tortoises. They have dry, scaly skin and typically live on land, though some live in water.

Amphibians include frogs, toads, salamanders, and caecilians (a lesser-known, worm-like group). Unlike reptiles, amphibians have moist skin and usually begin their lives in water before moving to land.

Together, there are roughly 10,000+ species of reptiles and 8,000+ species of amphibians on Earth — making this a vast and rich field.

Their work spans many areas:

  • Fieldwork: They go into forests, deserts, wetlands, and jungles to observe, track, and collect data on these animals in the wild.
  • Research: They study animal behaviour, feeding habits, reproduction, venom (in venomous snakes and lizards), and how these animals interact with their environment.
  • Conservation: Many reptiles and amphibians are endangered. Herpetologists work to protect their habitats and prevent extinction — amphibians in particular are disappearing faster than almost any other group of animals on Earth.
  • Medical research: Snake venom, for example, has led to life-saving medicines for blood clots and heart conditions. Herpetologists contribute to this kind of research.
  • Taxonomy: They discover and classify new species. Many frog and lizard species are still being identified today.

Herpetologists are typically found at:

  • Universities and research institutions
  • Natural history museums
  • Zoos and wildlife sanctuaries
  • Government wildlife and conservation agencies
  • Pharmaceutical and biomedical research labs
The science they practise is called herpetology — a branch of zoology (the study of animals). A herpetologist is therefore a type of zoologist with a specific specialisation.
A simple way to remember it

Think of it this way: just as a cardiologist is a doctor specialising in the heart, a herpetologist is a scientist specialising in reptiles and amphibians. The "-ologist" suffix always signals a specialist or expert in a particular field of study.
Why this word matters in everyday life

You're most likely to encounter this word in:

  • Nature documentaries (scientists featured in snake or frog episodes are often herpetologists)
  • News articles about endangered species
  • Discussions about antivenom or medical breakthroughs from animal venom
  • Wildlife conservation reports

In short: if someone is a herpetologist, they have dedicated their career to understanding the biology, behaviour, and survival of the world's reptiles and amphibians.
